episodes.title: How Much Tree Closes a Dome
episodes.description:
One dome, every triangle closed with wedges: four trees, or seven, and you choose which.

The dome's frame is 120 wedge members: 678 feet of wedge, cut from one log after another. Close every triangle with more wedges, laid in pairs with their points facing in, and the pairs can nest tight or open into a bowtie. Nested, a pair covers one wedge face; opened, two. That one choice moves the whole dome between 1,796 and 2,913 feet of wedge.

episodes.description:
What a dome should be.

episodes.title: Beyond the Dome: Building With Wedges
episodes.description:
The same wedges, other buildings.

The dome on this hill is framed from 120 wedges split from logs with one chainsaw. This film is about everything else those wedges can build. A zome, framed from the same pile. Square posts, made from wedges on demand. A roof whose pitch is already in the log. An octagon, a set of joints, and a seam that carries water. And it starts where every wedge does: with a log.

chapters.title: The skew is a roof pitch
The octagon is in the log
A zome from the same pile

episodes.title: Every Piece, Numbered: Filling the Triangles and Framing the Floor
episodes.description:
A triangle and a floor, cut by the numbers.

Two things are built from wood in this film. One of the dome's forty triangles, filled with wedges split from a log. And the floor the whole dome stands on, framed from five twenty-foot half trunks. Every piece of both has a number. Every number has a length, an angle, and a way of cutting it, worked out by one calculator and shown on the saw before anyone picks up a blade.

chapters.title: What is solved, what is assumed

episodes.title: The Panel Method: A Three-Frequency Dome, Framed on a Jig
episodes.description:
Same hill, two methods.

On this hill stand two domes framed two different ways. One is the wedge dome: 120 members split from logs with a chainsaw, carrying their angles in their own shape. The other is a three-frequency dome of framed panels: 105 triangles, each one its own small frame of sawn sticks, built flat on a jig, skinned in the shop, and screwed to its neighbours on site. It is how most small timber domes built from bought plans are made, and it is worth knowing properly.

chapters.title: Two ways to frame a dome

episodes.title: The Shop the Campaign Buys: A 10 x 5 Plasma Table and Its Router
episodes.description:
Two machine lines, one frame.

Part of what backing this project pays for is a shop. Not a building: two machines. A plasma table that cuts a whole sheet of steel into the panels of a dome, and a router that cuts the jigs and the wooden panels. This film is what those two machines are, what they make, and what they cost when you build them rather than buy them. Here is the first thing the table makes: one 120 by 60 inch sheet of plate, 40 panels.

episodes.title: Linseed Oil for a Dome: Uses, Limits and Method
episodes.description:
Where it earns a place in the build.

The Lost Handyman video offers 20 linseed oil tricks. Here we bring the useful ones into the wedge dome workshop. Start with the exposed interior wood, shelves, trim and hand tools. Then look at the seams, windows and weather skin, where a finish must work with the rest of the assembly. The source is a set of claims, not a comparison test. We will show the work, the quantities and the limits before calling anything a saving.
